keyPoints: Hysteroscopy is the gold standard for evaluation of intracavitary pathology in both premenopausal and postmenopausal patients
Office-based operative hysteroscopy allows immediate return to normal activities when NSAIDs alone are used for analgesia
Optimal timing for hysteroscopic procedures is early proliferative phase (menstrual days 4-11) when endometrium is thinnest
Office hysteroscopy is cost-effective, enhances physician productivity, and improves patient satisfaction
Cervical stenosis in premenopausal women may require cervical priming with misoprostol before hysteroscopy
Indications include evaluation and treatment of endometrial polyps, submucous myomas, uterine septa, and adhesions
Miniature hysteroscopes (3-5 mm) enable office procedures without cervical dilation in most patients
Fluid management monitoring is essential to prevent distension media complications during operative hysteroscopy
Nearly 450,000 US women undergo hysterectomy by age 60; only 10-15% are for gynecologic malignancy
Operative hysteroscopy is a safe and effective minimally invasive treatment for submucosal and intramural leiomyomas
FIGO classifies submucosal fibroids into type 0 (pedunculated), type 1 (<50% intramural), and type 2 (>=50% intramural)
Hysteroscopic myomectomy is most successful for type 0 and type 1 fibroids less than 4-5 cm
Fluid deficit monitoring is critical; maximum deficit threshold varies by distension media (isotonic vs hypotonic)
Preoperative GnRH agonist therapy for 2-3 months can reduce fibroid size and facilitate hysteroscopic resection
Two-stage procedures may be necessary for large type 2 fibroids to reduce perforation and fluid overload risk
Hysteroscopic myomectomy should be leveraged to reduce unnecessary hysterectomies in women with intracavitary fibroids
Intracavitary abnormalities (polyps, submucous fibroids, septa, adhesions) are present in 10-15% of subfertile women
Observational studies suggest higher pregnancy rates after hysteroscopic removal of intracavitary pathology
Cochrane review found insufficient high-quality RCT evidence to confirm hysteroscopic treatment improves live birth rates
Hysteroscopic removal of endometrial polyps before IUI may improve pregnancy outcomes based on limited evidence
Hysteroscopic metroplasty for uterine septum is widely performed but supported only by observational data
Adhesiolysis for intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) may restore fertility but lacks RCT evidence
More high-quality randomized trials are needed to establish the true fertility benefit of operative hysteroscopy

Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are the most common pelvic tumor in females [1,2]. Abnormal
uterine bleeding, the most common symptom associated with fibroids, is most frequent in
patients with tumors that abut the endometrium (lining of the uterine cavity), including
submucosal and some intramural fibroids [3-5]. This is likely due to distortion of the uterine
cavity and an increase in the bleeding surface of the endometrium [6]. Submucosal
leiomyomas, which derive from myometrial cells just below the endometrium, account for
leiomyomas. This has been largely replaced by hysteroscopic myomectomy, a minimally
invasive surgical procedure that effectively and safely removes these lesions [4,7].
Hysteroscopic myomectomy is reviewed here. General principles of hysteroscopy and
abdominal approaches to myomectomy are discussed separately. (See "Hysteroscopy

INTRODUCTION Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) refers to any uterine bleeding in a menopausal patient (other than the expected cyclic bleeding that occurs in patients taking combined [ie, estrogen-progestin], cyclic, postmenopausal hormone therapy).
As PMB is the cardinal sign of endometrial carcinoma, all postmenopausal patients with unanticipated PMB should be evaluated for endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma.
More Per this document, however, the cause of bleeding in such patients is the result of a benign condition, such as endometrial polyps or atrophy.

The etiologies and evaluation of postmenopausal patients with uterine bleeding, as well as patients near the end of the perimenopausal transition with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), will be reviewed here.
The evaluation and management of postmenopausal patients with a nonuterine source of vaginal bleeding, as well as premenopausal patients with AUB, are discussed separately.

ETIOLOGY The differential diagnosis of bleeding in postmenopausal patients is less broad than that for abnormal bleeding in premenopausal patients since the various causes of anovulation are not relevant.
In two studies including gynecologically asymptomatic breast cancer patients prior to administration of adjuvant therapy, the baseline risk of an endometrial abnormality was 17 to 18 percent [7,8].
As with postmenopausal patients with bleeding, the most common abnormalities were atrophy and polyps.
clinicalPearls: Ofﬁce-based operative hysteroscopy allows patients to resume activities immediately and successfully integrates clinical practice into a “see and treat” modality, avoiding the added risks of anesthesia and the inconvenience of the operating room.

Those who do not offer this proce- dure to their patients may believe that their patient population would not beneﬁt from the procedure, or that ofﬁce hyster- oscopy requires special expertise.
We discuss preoperative evaluation, fluid management, postop- erative complications, preventative measures, and hysteroscopic outcomes.

In addition, hysterectomy may permanently alter a women’s pelvic floor anatomy, fertility, and for some their psyche, and is associ- ated with greater morbidity, higher health care costs, and other downstream impacts on patient health and quality of life.
